questions.explanation: Correct: app registration = application object, one global definition in the home tenant, holding the Application (client) ID, redirect URIs, secrets, and requested API permissions. Enterprise application = service principal, one per tenant that uses the app, holding consent, user assignment, and sign-in. Application ID is the same in every tenant; Object ID differs per tenant because each service principal is a different object. The first option reverses the IDs. The third is wrong — customers do not re-register the app. The fourth swaps the two objects' jobs.
options: The app registration and the enterprise application are the same object, with the same Object ID in every tenant

The app registration is the application object — the single blueprint in the home tenant. Each customer tenant gets its own enterprise application, which is a service principal. The Application (client) ID is the same everywhere; the Object ID is different in each tenant
Each customer tenant must create its own app registration with a new Application ID
Enterprise applications hold the app's secrets and redirect URIs; app registrations hold user assignments
questions.question: A developer builds a SaaS app, carbonops.cloud, registers it in their home tenant, and a customer tenant starts using it with Microsoft sign-in. A support engineer claims the app is 'the same object everywhere'. Which statement is correct?
questions.source_quote: The application object is the global representation of your application for use across all tenants, and the service principal is the local representation for use in a specific tenant.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: governance happens in the customer tenant, on that tenant's enterprise application (service principal): limit API permissions / consent, assign owners, apply Conditional Access to the application, and monitor its sign-in and audit logs. The home-tenant app registration is the blueprint — it cannot enforce per-customer limits. Deleting the registration would break the app for everyone. A directory read role is not app governance.
options: Only in the developer's home tenant, by editing the app registration — customer tenants cannot limit it
In the customer tenant, on the enterprise application / service principal for that app — for example, by limiting its API permissions, assigning owners, and applying Conditional Access to it
By deleting the app registration in the home tenant
By assigning the app the Directory Reader role
questions.question: A customer tenant uses the SaaS app, and the app requests OneDrive API access. The customer wants to limit the app to one folder, not the whole OneDrive account. Where is that governed?
questions.source_quote: The service principal object defines what the app can actually do in the specific tenant, who can access the app, and what resources the app can access.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: a user-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be assigned to multiple resources. System-assigned is tied to one resource and deleted when that resource is deleted, so it cannot be shared with the VM. The first and third options assume sharing of a system-assigned identity. The fourth is false — managed identities are the recommended way to access Key Vault without stored credentials.
options: System-assigned on the Function — it can be shared with the VM because both are in the same tenant
User-assigned — a standalone identity that can be assigned to both the Function and the VM; a system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it
System-assigned on the VM — the Function can use the VM's identity over the network
Neither — managed identities cannot access Key Vault, you must store a client secret in code
questions.question: An Azure Function needs to read secrets from Key Vault. A VM in another resource group also needs to read the same secrets. Which managed identity design is correct, and why?
questions.source_quote: User-assigned managed identities can be used by multiple resources.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: a managed identity authenticates — it proves which identity is calling. Authorisation is separate: you must grant it an Azure RBAC role (or Key Vault access policy) on the target vault. Enabling Conditional Access does not grant vault access. App registration is a different identity type. Granting the human user a role does not grant the managed identity anything.
options: Enable Conditional Access for the managed identity
Assign an Azure RBAC role (for example, Key Vault Secrets User) to the managed identity on the vault — the identity authenticates, but authorisation comes from RBAC
Register the managed identity as an app registration in the home tenant
Give the VM's user a Global Administrator role
questions.question: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on a VM. The VM still gets 'Forbidden' from Key Vault. What is the missing step?
questions.source_quote: Managed identities eliminate the need for developers to manage these credentials. Applications can use managed identities to obtain Microsoft Entra tokens without having to manage any credentials.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: under the Microsoft-managed consent policy, risky delegated permissions such as Mail.ReadWrite and Calendars.ReadWrite are blocked for user self-consent and routed to admin consent. Control lives in Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions. The first option describes the old wide-open default. The third is wrong — there is a request path. The fourth is wrong — after admin consent, ordinary users can use the app.
options: The user can consent themselves — delegated permissions never need admin consent

The user is blocked from self-consent for those risky permissions and must request admin consent; this is controlled in Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions > User consent settings / Admin consent settings
The app is blocked tenant-wide automatically, with no request path
Only Global Administrators can use the app at all, even after admin consent
questions.question: A user tries to connect a third-party AI meeting assistant that requests Mail.ReadWrite and Calendars.ReadWrite (delegated). Your tenant uses the Microsoft-managed consent policy. What is the expected behaviour, and where is it controlled?
questions.source_quote: Users can consent to applications from verified publishers or your organization, but only for permissions you select.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: Learn is explicit — designating someone as a reviewer does not elevate their privileges. The reviewer must separately hold the permissions required to grant the requested consent — for Microsoft Graph application permissions, that is a highly privileged approval. The first option assumes the designation grants power. The third invents a delegated/application split for this rule. The fourth is wrong — the requester does not approve their own request.
options: Yes — being designated a reviewer automatically gives them permission to grant consent
No — designating someone as a reviewer does not elevate their privileges; they must separately hold the permissions required to grant that consent
Yes, but only for delegated permissions, not application permissions
No — only the user who requested consent can approve it
questions.question: You designate a help-desk lead as a reviewer in the admin consent workflow. A user requests consent for an app requesting Application.Read.All (application permission). Can the reviewer approve it?
questions.source_quote: To approve requests, a reviewer must have the permissions required to grant admin consent for the application requested. Simply designating them as a reviewer doesn't elevate their privileges.
questions.source_title: Configure the admin consent workflow - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: if an application requires assignment, its permissions require admin consent regardless of whether they would otherwise allow user consent. The first option treats User.Read as always user-consentable, ignoring the assignment gate. The third and fourth invent other causes — the trigger is Assignment required = Yes.
options: A bug — User.Read never needs admin consent
If an application requires assignment, its permissions require admin consent regardless of whether they would otherwise allow user consent
The user is a guest, and guests always need admin consent
The app registration is in another tenant, so all permissions need admin consent
questions.question: An enterprise application is configured with 'Assignment required? Yes.' A user who is assigned to the app tries to sign in and is asked to request admin consent, even though the app only requests User.Read (a low-impact delegated permission). Why?
questions.source_quote: User access to applications can still be limited, even when tenant-wide admin consent is already granted. Configure the application's properties to require user assignment to limit user access to the application.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: registering an app creates both an application object and a service principal object in the home tenant automatically (portal registration does both steps). The application object is the blueprint; the service principal is the local instance. The other options invent a manual second step or a missing object.
options: Both are created automatically in the home tenant when the app is registered
Only the application object is created; the service principal must be created manually in every tenant including the home tenant
Only the service principal is created; the application object is created when the first user signs in
Neither is created until an administrator grants admin consent
questions.question: A developer registers a new application in the Microsoft Entra admin center. What objects exist in the home tenant immediately after registration?
questions.source_quote: If you register an application, an application object and a service principal object are automatically created in your home tenant.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: changes to the application object are reflected in its service principal only in the home tenant; each customer tenant's service principal is its own object governed by that tenant's consent. The other options wrongly assume home-tenant edits propagate everywhere or that customers cannot govern the app locally.
options: The change propagates to every customer tenant's service principal automatically
The change deletes all customer service principals and they must be recreated
The change applies to no service principal anywhere — app objects and service principals are unrelated
The change is reflected only in the home tenant's service principal; each customer tenant's service principal is governed locally by that tenant
questions.question: A SaaS vendor changes the redirect URIs on their application object in their home tenant. A customer tenant admin asks whether this changes the enterprise application in their tenant. What is the correct answer?
questions.source_quote: Any changes that you make to your application object are also reflected in its service principal object in the application's home tenant only (the tenant where it was registered).
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: deactivation prevents new token issuance while preserving the application object and service principal for investigation or future reactivation — the right move for a suspected compromise. Deletion is permanent and, if the app object is restored, its home service principal is not restored with it. Doing nothing or only removing user assignments leaves the app able to get tokens.
options: Delete the application object immediately, because deletion is reversible with one click
Remove all user assignments and leave the app active — that stops token issuance
Deactivate the application, which prevents new token issuance while preserving the objects for investigation or future reactivation
Change the application's client secret, which immediately invalidates all existing tokens
questions.question: A third-party app's service principal shows suspicious sign-ins. You need to stop it getting new tokens right now, but preserve everything for investigation and possible reactivation. What do you do?
questions.source_quote: For applications that need temporary suspension rather than permanent deletion, you can deactivate the application. Deactivation prevents new token issuance while preserving the application object and service principal for investigation or future reactivation.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: there are three types of service principal — Application (the local instance of a global app object), Managed identity (representing a managed identity, with no associated app object), and Legacy (an app created before app registrations, with no associated app registration). The other options invent types or deny the managed identity type.
options: Application, Managed identity, and Legacy
Application and User only
Application, Guest, and Member only
There is only one type — every service principal is an application instance
questions.question: An auditor asks you to classify three service principals: one for a registered SaaS app, one for a managed identity on a VM, and one for an app created before app registrations existed. Which three types are these?
questions.source_quote: Application - This type of service principal is the local representation, or application instance, of a global application object in a single tenant or directory.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: a service principal representing a managed identity has no associated app object — unlike the Application type — and cannot be updated or modified directly. It is not an app registration, it is not owned by the developer, and it is not deletable through the app registrations blade.
options: It has an app object that the developer can edit in App registrations
It can be updated directly like any other service principal
It is owned by the application developer and follows the app's lifecycle
It has no associated app object and cannot be updated or modified directly
questions.question: A developer tries to edit the service principal for a managed identity in App registrations and cannot find it. Why?
questions.source_quote: A service principal representing a managed identity doesn't have an associated app object (unlike the Application type above). Service principals representing managed identities can be granted access and permissions, but can't be updated or modified directly.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: the system-assigned service principal is tied to the resource's lifecycle — when the resource is deleted, Azure automatically deletes the service principal. The identity cannot outlive the resource, cannot be transferred, and does not need manual cleanup.
options: The identity survives and can be attached to a replacement VM
The identity survives but loses all role assignments
Azure automatically deletes the service principal when the resource is deleted
The identity is converted to a user-assigned managed identity automatically
questions.question: You delete a VM that had a system-assigned managed identity with Key Vault access. What happens to the identity?
questions.source_quote: The service principal is tied to the lifecycle of that Azure resource. When the Azure resource is deleted, Azure automatically deletes the service principal for you.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: the system-assigned service principal's name is always the same as the Azure resource it was created for (and for a deployment slot, <app-name>/slots/<slot-name>). It is not a random GUID name, not the tenant name, and not chosen by the admin.
options: The service principal is named after the Azure resource it belongs to
The service principal gets a random GUID name unrelated to the resource
The service principal is named after the tenant
The administrator chooses the name at creation time
questions.question: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on an App Service named invoicing-api. What is the managed identity's service principal called in Entra ID?
questions.source_quote: The name of the system-assigned service principal is always the same as the name of the Azure resource it's created for.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: user-assigned managed identities are provisioned independently from compute, can be assigned to multiple resources, and are the recommended type for Microsoft services — exactly the pre-authorisation, frequent-recycling scenario. System-assigned identities cannot be shared and die with the resource; a stored secret reintroduces credential management.
options: A system-assigned identity on each VM, re-authorised every time a VM is recycled
A client secret stored in Key Vault and injected at startup
A user-assigned managed identity, pre-authorised on the vault and assigned to each VM as it is created — user-assigned is the recommended type for this pattern
A single service principal with a certificate that every VM shares
questions.question: A scale set recycles VMs daily, and every VM needs the same Key Vault access with permissions that stay consistent across recycles. Which identity design fits?
questions.source_quote: User-assigned managed identities, which are provisioned independently from compute and can be assigned to multiple compute resources, are the recommended managed identity type for Microsoft services.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: managed identities remove credential management entirely — credentials are not even accessible to you. There is no secret to rotate, no certificate to renew, and no password to store; the platform obtains tokens for the identity. The other options describe the old secret-based pattern that managed identities replace.
options: The developer must rotate the managed identity's secret every 90 days
The developer must store the managed identity's certificate in Key Vault
There are no credentials to manage or rotate — credentials are not even accessible to you
The developer must renew the managed identity's password annually
questions.question: A developer asks for the runbook on rotating a managed identity's credentials. What is the correct answer?
questions.source_quote: You don't need to manage credentials. Credentials aren't even accessible to you.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: workload identity federation lets a managed identity act as a credential on an Entra ID app — the recommended credential-free path — with a limit of 20 federated identity credentials when using managed identities as FIC. It is not a password, not unlimited, and not a replacement for the app object.
options: A managed identity can be used as a federated identity credential on an Entra ID app, with a limit of 20 FICs — the recommended credential-free path
A managed identity can be used as a password on an app, with no limit
A managed identity cannot be used as a credential on an app at all
A managed identity replaces the app object, so no app registration is needed
questions.question: A workload running on Azure compute with a managed identity needs to act as an Entra ID application without storing any secret. What is the supported approach, and what is its limit?
questions.source_quote: Workload Identity Federation enables using a managed identity as a credential, just like certificate or password, on Entra ID Applications. Whenever an Entra ID app is required, this is the recommended way to be credential-free. There's a limit of 20 FICs when using managed identities as FIC on an Entra ID App.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: delegated permissions let an application act on behalf of the signed-in user, accessing only what that user can access. Application permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in. The other options reverse the two or invent a user-presence requirement for application permissions.
options: Delegated permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in; application permissions require a user
Both types require a signed-in user at all times
Delegated permissions are only for Microsoft's own apps; third-party apps can only use application permissions
Delegated permissions let the app act on behalf of the signed-in user, limited to what that user can access; application permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in
questions.question: A backup service needs to read all mailboxes overnight with no user signed in, while a reporting add-in only reads the signed-in user's own mailbox. Which permission types do they need?
questions.source_quote: A user can authorize an application to access some data at the protected resource, while acting as that user. The permissions that allow this type of access are called "delegated permissions."
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: user consent is possible only where it is allowed for the application and for the set of permissions requested — if user consent is disabled, or users are not allowed to consent for the requested permissions, they are not prompted for consent. The app is not blocked tenant-wide; it is routed to admin consent. And consent is not automatic for low-impact permissions when user consent is disabled.
options: The user is prompted for consent anyway, because low-impact permissions always allow user consent
The app is blocked tenant-wide and can never be used
User consent is possible only where it is allowed for the application and the requested permissions — with user consent disabled, the user is not prompted and must request admin consent
The user can consent, but only if they are a guest user
questions.question: Your tenant disables user consent entirely. A user tries to sign in to an app requesting only User.Read. What happens?
questions.source_quote: User consent by nonadministrators is possible only in organizations where user consent is allowed for the application and for the set of permissions the application requires. If user consent is disabled, or users aren't allowed to consent for the requested permissions, they aren't prompted for consent.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: tenant-wide admin consent is a sensitive operation, potentially giving the publisher access to significant portions of the organisation's data or permission to do highly privileged operations — role management, full access to all mailboxes or all sites, full user impersonation. The other options understate the blast radius or invent a limitation that does not exist.
options: It is a sensitive operation that can give the application's publisher access to significant portions of the organisation's data or permission to do highly privileged operations
It only affects the administrator who grants it, not other users
It can be undone automatically after 30 days with no action needed
It only grants the permissions the first user requested, not the full set the app asks for
questions.question: An administrator is about to grant tenant-wide admin consent to a new SaaS app requesting Mail.ReadWrite for all mailboxes. What should they understand before clicking grant?
questions.source_quote: Granting admin consent on behalf of an organization is a sensitive operation, potentially allowing the application's publisher access to significant portions of the organization's data, or the permission to do highly privileged operations. Examples of such operations might be role management, full access to all mailboxes or all sites, and full user impersonation.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: after admin consent is granted on behalf of the organisation, users are not prompted for consent for that application — unless the app later requests another permission the administrator has not granted, in which case the user may be prompted again. Consent is not per-session, not limited to admins, and not permanent for new permissions.
options: Users are prompted for consent on every sign-in, even after admin consent
Only administrators can use the app after admin consent; regular users still need to consent
Admin consent expires after 90 days and must be renewed
Users are not prompted for consent after admin consent — unless the app requests another permission the administrator has not granted
questions.question: You grant tenant-wide admin consent for a reporting app. A month later a user is prompted for consent again when opening the same app. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.source_quote: After an administrator grants admin consent on behalf of the organization, users aren't prompted for consent for that application. In certain cases, a user might be prompted for consent even after an administrator grants consent. An example might be if an application requests another permission that the administrator hasn't granted.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: the admin consent workflow gives users a way to request admin consent when they are not allowed to consent themselves — the user sees an 'Approval required' window, submits a justification, and the designated reviewers are notified. It is not automatic approval, not a block with no recourse, and not a self-approval path.
options: The user is blocked permanently and must ask IT to register the app for them
The user can approve the request themselves by re-entering their password
The user sees an 'Approval required' window, submits a justification, and the designated reviewers are notified
The request is sent to Microsoft support for approval
questions.question: User consent is disabled in your tenant. A user tries to sign in to a new app and cannot consent. The admin consent workflow is enabled. What happens next?
questions.source_quote: The admin consent workflow gives users a way to request admin consent for applications when they aren't allowed to consent themselves. When the admin consent workflow is enabled, users are presented with an "Approval required" window for requesting admin approval for access to the application.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: only Global Administrators can approve admin consent requests for apps requesting Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions) — a reviewer designated in the workflow cannot approve those, even if they can review the request. The other options give the reviewer power they do not have.
options: Only Global Administrators can approve admin consent requests for apps requesting Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions)
Any designated reviewer can approve them
Any Application Administrator can approve them
The requesting user can approve them if no reviewer responds within 24 hours
questions.question: A user requests consent for an app that needs Microsoft Graph application permissions (app roles). The designated reviewer is a help-desk lead. Who can actually approve this request?
questions.source_quote: only Global Administrators can approve admin consent requests for apps requesting for Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions).
questions.source_title: Configure the admin consent workflow - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: enabling the workflow requires a Global Administrator to turn it on, and it can take up to an hour for the workflow to become enabled — the team should wait rather than re-creating it or assuming it failed. A Conditional Access Administrator cannot enable it, and reviewers cannot enable it for themselves.
options: A Conditional Access Administrator can enable it instantly
Any designated reviewer can enable it for themselves
It is enabled automatically as soon as the first request is submitted
A Global Administrator must turn it on, and it can take up to an hour for the workflow to become enabled
questions.question: You configure the admin consent workflow at 9 a.m. At 9:15 a.m. a user still sees no 'Approval required' option. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.source_quote: You must be a Global Administrator to turn on the admin consent workflow. It can take up to an hour for the workflow to become enabled.
questions.source_title: Configure the admin consent workflow - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: the admin consent workflow gives admins a secure way to grant access to applications that require admin approval — when a user cannot provide consent, they send a request for admin approval, the request goes by email to the designated reviewers, a reviewer acts, and the user is notified. It is not an automatic grant, not a user self-approval, and not a block with no path.
options: The application is granted consent automatically after 24 hours
The user grants consent to themselves by confirming twice
The user sends a request for admin approval, the designated reviewers receive it by email, a reviewer acts, and the user is notified
The request goes to the application's publisher for approval
questions.question: How does the admin consent workflow actually move a request from a blocked user to a decision?
questions.source_quote: The admin consent workflow gives admins a secure way to grant access to applications that require admin approval. When a user tries to access an application but is unable to provide consent, they can send a request for admin approval. The request is sent via email to admins who are designated as reviewers. A reviewer takes action on the request, and the user is notified of the action.
questions.source_title: Configure the admin consent workflow - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: you can add or remove reviewers, but a reviewer retains the ability to review requests made while they were designated, and will keep receiving expiration reminders for those requests after removal; new reviewers are not assigned to requests created before they were set as reviewers. Removal is not retroactive.
options: A removed reviewer retains the ability to review requests made while they were designated, and keeps receiving expiration reminders for those requests
Removal is retroactive — all of the reviewer's pending requests are cancelled immediately
New reviewers are automatically assigned to all old requests
A removed reviewer can still approve new requests for 30 days
questions.question: You remove a help-desk lead from the admin consent reviewer list. A request they were already reviewing is still pending. What happens to that request?
questions.source_quote: A current limitation of this feature is that a reviewer retains the ability to review requests that were made while they were designated as a reviewer and will receive expiration reminder emails for those requests after they're removed from the reviewers list. Additionally, new reviewers won't be assigned to requests that were created before they were set as a reviewer.
questions.source_title: Configure the admin consent workflow - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: consent can be granted on behalf of a single user through the Microsoft Graph API instead of the whole organisation — the alternative to tenant-wide consent when only one person needs the app. It is not possible through the portal's tenant-wide grant alone, and it does not require disabling user consent tenant-wide.
options: It is impossible — consent is always tenant-wide or nothing
Disable user consent tenant-wide and the single user will be covered
Ask the user to consent themselves, which always works for any permission
Use the Microsoft Graph API to grant consent to delegated permissions on behalf of that single user
questions.question: One executive needs a niche app that requests a delegated permission. You do not want to grant tenant-wide admin consent for the whole organisation. What is the supported alternative?
questions.source_quote: Instead of granting consent for an entire organization, an admin can also use the Microsoft Graph API to grant consent to delegated permissions on behalf of a single user.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: requiring user assignment limits who can use the app even after tenant-wide admin consent — consent and assignment are separate controls. Admin consent does not override assignment, assignment is not removed by consent, and guests are not automatically included.
options: Tenant-wide admin consent overrides assignment, so all users can sign in
User assignment is removed automatically once admin consent is granted
Requiring user assignment still limits access to assigned users only, even after tenant-wide admin consent
Only guest users are affected by assignment; members bypass it after admin consent
questions.question: You grant tenant-wide admin consent for an app that has 'Assignment required? Yes' with only the Finance group assigned. A user outside Finance tries to sign in. What happens?
questions.source_quote: User access to applications can still be limited, even when tenant-wide admin consent is already granted. Configure the application's properties to require user assignment to limit user access to the application.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: the Enterprise applications page lists and manages the service principals in a tenant — permissions, user-consented permissions, who consented, and sign-in information. App registrations manages application objects, not service principals. The other options point at the wrong blades.
options: The Enterprise applications page, which lists and manages the service principals in the tenant
The App registrations page, which lists service principals
The Conditional Access policies page, which lists service principals
The Access reviews page, which lists service principals
questions.question: A security analyst needs to see a SaaS app's permissions, who consented to them, and its sign-in activity in your tenant. Where do they look?
questions.source_quote: You can use the Enterprise applications page in the Microsoft Entra admin center to list and manage the service principals in a tenant. You can see the service principal's permissions, user consented permissions, which users have done that consent, sign in information, and more.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: deleting an application object also deletes its home tenant service principal, but restoring the application object through the app registrations UI will not restore its corresponding service principal — the recovery is incomplete. The other options assume a clean restore that Learn explicitly rules out.
options: Deleting the app object only deletes the customer service principals, not the home one
Restoring the app object restores its service principal automatically
Deleting the app object has no effect on any service principal
Deleting the app object also deletes its home tenant service principal, and restoring the app object will not restore that service principal
questions.question: An administrator deletes an application object by mistake, then restores it from the app registrations UI. The app still does not work in the home tenant. Why?
questions.source_quote: Deleting an application object will also delete its home tenant service principal object. However, restoring that application object through the app registrations UI won't restore its corresponding service principal.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: a single-tenant application has only one service principal (in its home tenant), created and consented for use during registration. A multitenant application gets a service principal in each tenant where a user has consented to its use. The other options confuse the two models.
options: A single-tenant app has a service principal in every tenant in the world
A multitenant app has only one service principal, in its home tenant
A single-tenant app has only one service principal, in its home tenant; a multitenant app has a service principal in each tenant where a user has consented to its use
Both models create a new application object in every customer tenant
questions.question: Two apps are registered: one single-tenant, one multitenant. A user in a customer tenant consents to the multitenant app. How many service principals exist for each app, and where?
questions.source_quote: A single-tenant application has only one service principal (in its home tenant), created and consented for use during application registration. A multitenant application also has a service principal created in each tenant where a user from that tenant has consented to its use.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: a legacy service principal represents a legacy app created before app registrations were introduced or through legacy experiences — it can have credentials, service principal names, and reply URLs, but has no associated app registration and can only be used in the tenant where it was created. It is not a managed identity and cannot be moved between tenants.
options: It is a legacy service principal: it has no associated app registration and can only be used in the tenant where it was created
It is a managed identity that lost its Azure resource
It is an application-type service principal whose app object was deleted
It is a guest user account that was converted to an app
questions.question: You find a service principal with credentials and reply URLs but no app registration behind it, usable only in your tenant. What is it?
questions.source_quote: Legacy - This type of service principal represents a legacy app, which is an app created before app registrations were introduced or an app created through legacy experiences. A legacy service principal can have credentials, service principal names, reply URLs, and other properties that an authorized user can edit, but doesn't have an associated app registration. The service principal can only be used in the tenant where it was created.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: the application object describes how the service can issue tokens to access the application, the resources the application might need to access, and the actions the application can take. It does not hold user assignments (those live on the service principal) and does not store user passwords.
options: The user assignments for the app in each tenant
The passwords of the users who sign in to the app
The billing information for the app's publisher
How the service can issue tokens, which resources the application might need to access, and the actions the application can take
questions.question: A developer asks what the application object actually defines about their app. Which three things does it describe?
questions.source_quote: The application object describes three aspects of an application: How the service can issue tokens in order to access the application. The resources that the application might need to access. The actions that the application can take.
questions.source_title: Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID - Microsoft identity platform

questions.explanation: Correct: in Entra, workload identities are applications, service principals, and managed identities — the machine/non-human identities, alongside human identities. Devices are a separate identity type, and guest users are human identities, not workload identities.
options: Users, groups, and devices
Guest users, members, and administrators
Applications, service principals, and managed identities
Devices, printers, and IoT hubs only
questions.question: A zero-trust review asks you to inventory workload identities in Entra ID. Which three identity types make up workload identities?
questions.source_quote: In Microsoft Entra, workload identities are applications, service principals, and managed identities.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: managed identities can authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications — not just Microsoft services. They are not limited to Key Vault or storage, and they do not require a stored secret to call your own API.
options: Yes — managed identities can be used to authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications
No — managed identities only work with Microsoft-owned services such as Key Vault and Storage
No — your own applications can only accept client secrets
Yes, but only if the application is registered in a different tenant
questions.question: An API you built accepts Microsoft Entra authentication. A Function with a managed identity needs to call it. Can the Function authenticate with its managed identity, or must it use a client secret?
questions.source_quote: You can use managed identities to authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: by design, only the Azure resource the system-assigned identity belongs to can use it to request tokens — the identity cannot be shared or borrowed by another resource. The other options wrongly assume sharing is possible or that a network call can transfer the identity.
options: Yes — any resource in the same subscription can use it
Yes — any resource in the same resource group can use it
Yes — the Function can use it if it presents the VM's client secret
No — by design, only that Azure resource can use its system-assigned identity to request tokens
questions.question: A Function app tries to obtain a token using a VM's system-assigned managed identity. Will it work?
questions.source_quote: By design, only that Azure resource can use this identity to request tokens from Microsoft Entra ID.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: a managed identity replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords, and can replace certificates or other forms of authentication for service-to-service dependencies. The migration removes the stored credential entirely rather than moving it to a safer store.
options: Move the access key into Key Vault and keep using it
Rotate the access key more frequently and keep using it
Replace the access key with a managed identity, which replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords for service-to-service authentication
Keep the access key but restrict it by IP address only
questions.question: A legacy service authenticates to Storage with a shared access key stored in its configuration. The key has leaked twice. What is the recommended identity fix?
questions.source_quote: Managed identity replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords. In addition, managed identities can replace certificates or other forms of authentication for service-to-service dependencies.
questions.source_title: Managed identities for Azure resources - Managed identities for Azure resources

questions.explanation: Correct: the user-consent settings offer built-in options including disabling user consent, allowing consent only to verified publishers or your organisation for selected low-impact permissions, or allowing consent to all applications. The 'verified publisher plus selected low-impact permissions' option is the middle control between disabling consent and allowing everything.
options: Allow users to consent only to applications from verified publishers or your organisation, and only for permissions you select and classify as low impact
Allow users to consent to any application for any permission
Disable user consent entirely with no exceptions
Allow users to consent only to applications requesting application permissions
questions.question: Your tenant wants users to be able to adopt low-risk apps themselves, but not to consent to risky permissions from unknown publishers. Which user consent setting fits?
questions.source_quote: Users can consent to applications from verified publishers or your organization, but only for permissions you select. All users can consent only to applications published by a verified publisher and applications that are registered in your tenant. Users can consent only to the permissions classified as low impact.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: before granting tenant-wide admin consent, ensure you trust the application and its publisher for the level of access requested — if you are not confident who controls the app and why it requests the permissions, do not grant consent. The publisher's marketing, the user count, and the app's age are not the check.
options: The app has more than 10,000 users, so it must be safe
The publisher's website looks professional
The app was published recently, so it uses modern security
Ensure you trust the application and its publisher for the level of access requested — if you are not confident who controls the app and why it requests the permissions, do not grant consent
questions.question: An app from an unknown publisher requests full access to all mailboxes and all SharePoint sites. What check must an administrator perform before granting tenant-wide admin consent?
questions.source_quote: Before you grant tenant-wide admin consent, ensure that you trust the application and the application publisher, for the level of access you're granting. If you aren't confident that you understand who controls the application and why the application is requesting the permissions, don't grant consent.
questions.source_title: Overview of user and admin consent - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: when consent is required, the user is directed to the consent prompt if no previous record of user or admin consent exists for the required permissions — and once granted, the user usually does not have to consent again on future sign-ins. Consent is not per-session, not automatic, and not limited to the first tenant.
options: The user must consent on every sign-in, even after granting it once
The user is never prompted if the app is from a verified publisher
The user is directed to the consent prompt when no previous record of user or admin consent exists for the required permissions, and usually does not have to consent again on future sign-ins
The user is prompted only if they are a guest; members are never prompted
questions.question: A user signs in to a new app for the first time and sees a consent prompt. They accept. When will they see the prompt again for the same app and permissions?
questions.source_quote: If no previous record of user or admin consent for the required permissions exists, the user is directed to the consent prompt window to grant the application the requested permissions. If users are allowed to consent and they accept the requested permissions, the consent is recorded. The users usually don't have to consent again on future sign-ins to the same application.
